segments.title: Why Illustrious protected her hangar
segments.body: Ark Royal and other carriers also carried armour; Illustrious's distinctive feature was the inclusion of her hangar within the protected structure. British planners expected some attacks to get through, so they wanted damage to remain contained and repairable with limited facilities. That mattered especially in the Pacific, far from Britain's main industrial base. A carrier forced to return to Britain for repairs could spend additional months away from operations simply travelling to and from the repair yard.

evidence.note: Illustrious's armoured hangar was designed to contain expected damage when the carrier operated far from a major repair base.

segments.summary: Illustrious's armour scheme was meant to contain damage and preserve a carrier that might be far from a major repair base.

segments.title: Designing a carrier for aircraft not yet built
segments.body: A carrier hull might remain in service for twenty or thirty years while aircraft developed far more quickly. HMS Furious's decks supported several generations of torpedo bombers from Sopwith Cuckoos onward and fighters from Sopwith Camels to Hurricanes. Designers therefore had to preserve usefulness across aircraft that had yet to be built while judging whether future air power would strike directly or guide a battle fleet's guns. Illustrious's compromises record expectations about future naval aviation as well as the aircraft available in the 1930s.

evidence.note: Furious's successive torpedo bombers and fighters illustrate the multi-generation design horizon of a carrier hull.

segments.summary: HMS Furious shows why interwar designers had to anticipate decades of aircraft development instead of optimizing a carrier for one contemporary air group.

segments.title: Radar changes the carrier-defence problem
segments.body: Rear Admiral Reginald Henderson's 1936 argument linked fighter interception to the time available after an approaching raid was detected. Visual lookouts could struggle to detect fast aircraft early enough for fighters to launch and intercept. British development of beacon-assisted night strikes also gave planners reason to expect opponents to acquire similar capabilities, when aircraft would be harder to see approaching. Designers therefore reserved positions for radar before the equipment was mature. Illustrious became the first carrier fitted with early-warning radar before completion when Type 79Z went aboard. The set needed more power and supporting systems than expected, delaying completion by two months while those additions were fitted.

evidence.note: Henderson's interception argument, anticipated enemy night-strike capability, and the power and equipment changes needed to install Type 79Z.

segments.summary: Illustrious entered service with early-warning radar because visual lookouts could not give fighters reliable warning of fast or night attacks.

segments.title: Why Pacific repairs were harder for British carriers
segments.body: American and Japanese carriers operating in the Pacific had their home industrial bases on that ocean. Britain's plans began with Singapore as a theatre-entry base, with temporary bases to be established farther along the Chinese coast. Support in Australia would require investment, and facilities in India still left the fleet far from Britain's main naval industry and research establishments. Major repairs could therefore mean a long voyage back to Britain.

evidence.note: Singapore, planned temporary bases along China's coast, support in Australia and India, and the distance from Britain's main maritime industry.

segments.summary: Britain's Pacific plans depended on distant and developing support bases while most of its naval industry remained in Britain.

segments.title: Eleven battle honours on the Illustrious name
segments.body: Ships named Illustrious accumulated eleven battle honours across more than one hull. Genoa 1795, Basque Roads 1809, and Java 1811 belonged to earlier namesakes. The carrier added Taranto, Mediterranean, Malta Convoys, Diego Suarez, Salerno, Sabang, Palembang, and Okinawa. Eight of the name's eleven honours therefore came from this ship's service during World War II.

evidence.note: Three honours from earlier ships of the name and eight earned by this carrier during World War II.

segments.summary: Three honours came from earlier ships named Illustrious, while the 1940 carrier earned eight during World War II.

segments.title: The treaty compromise in Illustrious's design
segments.body: Illustrious's protected hangar lay between the lifts, with 4.5-inch armour on its sides and ends, a 3-inch flight deck and a 4.5-inch waterline belt. Fitting that protection into roughly 23,000 tons required compromises, including three shafts rather than four. Her machinery produced 111,000 shaft horsepower, and the quoted 30 knots was a designed speed at deep load, which should not automatically be treated as an absolute maximum. The nominal 36-aircraft complement usually meant twenty-four torpedo-spotter-reconnaissance aircraft and twelve fighters. The larger aircraft combined torpedo attack with spotting for battleships and reconnaissance, so aircraft counts alone concealed differences in fleet utility. A larger carrier combining Ark Royal's capacity with Illustrious's protection would have been closer to the Royal Navy's preference. Treaty limits also constrained how many such hulls the navy could obtain.

evidence.note: Armour thicknesses, three-shaft machinery, designed deep-load speed, the 24-plus-12 air group, and treaty limits on combined capability and hull numbers.

segments.summary: Armour, speed, machinery, and aircraft capacity reveal how treaty limits forced the Royal Navy to accept a compromise carrier.

segments.title: Damage control on top-heavy carriers
segments.body: One explanation for Ark Royal's loss gives more weight to damage-control training and preparation than to the ship's design. The early losses of Courageous and Glorious removed experienced carrier damage-control personnel, while further specialists had to leave serving ships to train replacements. Some incoming personnel had spent their careers in other ship types and regarded deliberate flooding as a last resort. Top-heavy carriers required prompt counter-flooding to balance incoming water, and the manuals already called for it. On Ark Royal, that action came too late. Better subdivision and torpedo protection remained possible design criticisms, but written procedures could only work if crews understood and accepted the carrier's different requirements.

evidence.note: Losses and instructor withdrawals reduced experienced carrier personnel, while delayed counter-flooding exposed the gap between written doctrine and accepted damage-control practice.

segments.summary: Carrier stability made rapid counter-flooding essential, but doctrine only worked when crews understood and trusted it.

segments.title: How inter-service separation consumed carrier space
segments.body: Internal carrier layout preserved the interwar division of naval aviation between the Royal Navy and Royal Air Force. In the 1920s, RAF demands for separate messes and other facilities introduced duplication into British carrier designs. Each requirement used only a modest amount of weight or space, but it added another constraint within the hull. Later integration of air-group personnel removed the institutional requirement for that separation.

evidence.note: RAF demands for separate facilities duplicated spaces within treaty-constrained interwar British carrier layouts.

segments.summary: Separate RAF messes and facilities consumed space and weight within British carrier designs.

segments.title: Breaking up an air attack
segments.body: Illustrious's eight twin 4.5-inch mountings were placed high enough to stay clear of heavy seas in the North Sea and Atlantic. Their position allowed broad arcs of fire without closing the flight deck during operations. Fighters disrupted incoming formations, heavy anti-aircraft guns broke them up further, and medium guns confronted isolated attackers. The aim was to prevent a concentrated raid from overwhelming the ship, even when every attacker could not be destroyed. Reconnaissance and spotting aircraft could also provide visual warning of approaching aircraft before radar became available.

evidence.note: Gun placement and layered fighter, heavy AA, and medium AA defence.

segments.summary: Fighters, heavy anti-aircraft fire, and pom-poms were designed to fragment a raid before it reached the carrier.

segments.title: The single-seat fighter Illustrious was meant to carry
segments.body: The intended air group included a compact single-seat fighter derived from Supermarine work related to the Spitfire. Without that aircraft, the Fleet Air Arm used the larger two-seat Fulmar for fighter and reconnaissance duties. With the smaller fighter, the estimated complement rises to eighteen fighters alongside twenty-four torpedo-spotter-reconnaissance aircraft. The Supermarine proposal is an example whose surviving sketches, timing, and specifications appear to fit the carrier programme; other aircraft companies also seem to have been involved. Its proposed gull wings offered strength and extra clearance for carrier landings. The air-group estimate therefore depends on an aircraft that was never available for Illustrious's wartime service.

evidence.note: The intended compact Supermarine fighter could have given Illustrious an estimated eighteen fighters alongside twenty-four torpedo-spotter-reconnaissance aircraft, while the larger two-seat Fulmar occupied more space.
The Supermarine example is inferred from surviving designs and programme timing, with other manufacturers apparently involved and gull wings proposed for strength and carrier clearance.

segments.summary: The intended compact Supermarine naval fighter helps explain why Illustrious's air group differed from the mix of aircraft envisaged during design.

segments.title: Why a carrier's aircraft total can mislead
segments.body: The Royal Navy's nominal air group counted the maximum number of fully assembled aircraft that could be stored in the hangar. It excluded boxed aircraft and did not assume that exposed aircraft could remain safely on deck in rough northern or Atlantic waters. Deck parking had cost aircraft during trials in the 1920s, although calmer conditions in the Mediterranean, Indian Ocean, and Pacific made it more practical. Illustrious also relied on Unicorn for maintenance functions that Ark Royal carried herself, another concession to weight limits. Aircraft totals therefore reflected the types carried, the operating area, and the support available.

evidence.note: British air-group counts excluded boxed aircraft, rough seas limited deck parking, and Unicorn supplied maintenance capacity that Illustrious could not accommodate within her weight limit.

segments.summary: British carrier air-group figures counted aircraft housed in the hangar, not every aircraft that calmer seas might allow on deck.

segments.title: The Ten Year Rule and Illustrious's timing
segments.body: The Ten Year Rule assumed that Britain would face no major war for ten years and officially ended in 1932. The practical brakes on rearmament did not come off until 1937, the year Illustrious was laid down. Her design therefore emerged while the Royal Navy was trying to recover from years of constrained planning. That timing helps explain why carrier and aircraft programmes still carried older assumptions as war approached.

evidence.note: The Ten Year Rule formally ended in 1932, while rearmament restraints eased in practice by 1937, when Illustrious was laid down.

segments.summary: Illustrious was laid down in 1937, the year the practical restraints left by the Ten Year Rule finally eased.

segments.title: Why Illustrious worked up at Bermuda
segments.body: Illustrious had been expected to work up around Plymouth, but Germany's conquest of France made Plymouth and the Bay of Biscay unsuitable for preparing a new carrier. The work-up moved to Bermuda and was completed by July 1940. After returning to the Clyde, she underwent a minor refit to correct faults found during training. She then embarked Rear Admiral Lister and sailed for the Mediterranean with fifteen Fulmars and eighteen Swordfish.

evidence.note: Bermuda replaced the planned Plymouth work-up after the fall of France, followed by defect correction on the Clyde and departure for the Mediterranean.

segments.summary: Germany's conquest of France made the planned work-up around Plymouth and the Bay of Biscay unsafe, so Illustrious trained at Bermuda.

segments.title: Illustrious enters the Mediterranean war
segments.body: Illustrious completed her Bermuda work-up and a corrective refit on the Clyde before sailing for the Mediterranean with fifteen Fulmars and eighteen Swordfish. Force H escorted her and Valiant into the Mediterranean during Operation Hats. Fulmars claimed five Italian bombers and the carrier's guns accounted for two more aircraft before she met the Mediterranean Fleet beyond Malta. Swordfish from Illustrious and Eagle attacked Rhodes, followed later by a night raid on Benghazi. These operations combined fighter defence with attacks on ports and shipping before Taranto.

evidence.note: Bermuda work-up, Operation Hats, Rhodes, and Benghazi.

segments.summary: After working up at Bermuda, Illustrious entered the Mediterranean under Force H escort and began operations against Italian aircraft and ports.

segments.title: Why Fulmars needed a standing combat air patrol
segments.body: The Fulmar could not gain altitude as quickly as the fleet needed when enemy aircraft approached. Keeping a combat air patrol aloft put fighters in position before an attack developed. Newly launched alert aircraft could then replace the patrol while the fighters already at height intercepted the attackers. Illustrious helped develop this practice alongside Ark Royal, whose Skuas faced a similar problem. Carriers using Sea Gladiators had less difficulty getting their fighters to altitude.

evidence.note: Fulmar climb limitations encouraged permanent patrols, with alert aircraft replacing the fighters already on station.

segments.summary: The Fulmar's limited climb performance encouraged carriers to keep fighters at altitude and use newly launched aircraft to replace the patrol.

segments.title: Benghazi: a night strike combining bombs and mines
segments.body: Fifteen Swordfish attacked Benghazi during the night of 16-17 September. They laid mines at the harbour entrance while also attacking ships inside. The strike destroyed an Italian destroyer and two freighters totalling roughly 10,000 gross register tons. Another destroyer later struck one of the mines and sank. Attacks on smaller ports had demonstrated British night-attack capability before Taranto, although they may also have encouraged an assumption that Britain would avoid the main Italian base.

evidence.note: The Benghazi night raid combined direct attacks on shipping with harbour-entrance mines, accounting for two destroyers and two freighters.

segments.summary: Fifteen Swordfish attacked Benghazi at night, destroying shipping and laying mines that sank another destroyer.

segments.title: Attrition frustrated British multi-carrier doctrine
segments.body: Illustrious and Eagle were worked hard because neither ship alone provided the desired combination of fighters, strike aircraft, and maintenance capacity. Eagle's condition kept her out of the Taranto attack, while later damage to Illustrious and Formidable continued the cycle of single-carrier operations. The Royal Navy had practiced coordinating several flight decks throughout the interwar period. Force availability across a global war remained the limiting factor, so earlier procurement and maintenance decisions shaped later operational choices.

evidence.note: Eagle's overwork, the limited Taranto force, and later carrier damage kept Britain from applying its prewar multi-carrier doctrine consistently.

segments.summary: The Royal Navy had practiced operating several carriers together, but losses, damage, and worldwide commitments repeatedly denied it enough available flight decks.

segments.title: Bomb damage exposes an armoured carrier's weak points
segments.body: The lift areas beyond the main armoured hangar were particularly vulnerable to attack. Four, possibly five, bombs struck near the after lift, and one entered the hangar and shredded a fire curtain intended to confine a fire to one of its three sections. Near misses also damaged hull plating through underwater shock waves. Illustrious escaped via Alexandria, Durban, and Norfolk before further work in Britain prepared her for newer aircraft. Differences between British and American Imperial measurements prompted checks on the Norfolk repairs, which found some discrepancies but nothing too major.

evidence.note: Direct hits around the after lift, a destroyed hangar fire curtain, near-miss damage to hull plating, and repairs through Alexandria, Durban, Norfolk, and Britain.

segments.summary: Direct hits near the after lift damaged Illustrious's hangar, while near misses damaged hull plating and contributed to a long repair journey.

segments.title: A shipboard fire tests the aircraft-replacement system
segments.body: Illustrious sailed for the Indian Ocean with Martlets, Swordfish, and two Fulmars, then suffered an onboard fire that destroyed eleven aircraft and killed one crewman. The fire caused little serious damage to the ship, although the crewman's death was apparently caused by smoke inhalation. Repairs at Freetown replaced the destroyed aircraft, and twelve additional Martlet IIs came aboard from HMS Archer. The complement rose to 47 aircraft. Smaller fighters allowed more aircraft aboard than the larger multi-seat types previously available.

evidence.note: An onboard fire killed a crewman and destroyed eleven aircraft before repairs at Freetown and replacement Martlets from Archer restored Illustrious's air group.

segments.summary: A fire en route to the Indian Ocean destroyed eleven aircraft and killed a crewman, but repairs and replacements at Freetown restored and enlarged the air group.

segments.title: Why long-range carrier aircraft carried navigators
segments.body: The Fulmar's two-seat arrangement suited its intended work as an escort fighter for long-range strikes. Returning to a carrier at night required reaching the expected rendezvous area before the ship's limited-power homing beacon could help. Finding the ship also depended on synchronizing the aircraft's watch with the beacon's rotation. A navigator in the rear seat could keep checking the route and calculations while the pilot flew in darkness, faced enemy attacks, and lined up for a strike. Multi-seat aircraft therefore addressed navigation demands that became especially difficult during long-range and night operations.

evidence.note: The Fulmar's long-range escort role and night recovery using the carrier's navigation plan, a limited-power beacon, and synchronized watches.

segments.summary: A dedicated navigator helped aircraft reach a moving carrier's rendezvous area and use its rotating beacon after a night strike.

segments.title: Shipboard workshops convert a Martlet's wings
segments.body: Illustrious received ASV radar components for her replacement Swordfish while carrying an air group of 47 aircraft. Engineers aboard also converted a fixed-wing Martlet I into an aircraft with folding wings. This work depended on the engineering facilities built into British carriers. Spare wings, engines, and fuselages allowed crews to rebuild and maintain aircraft at sea. Those components did not appear in the air-group total, so the number of assembled aircraft concealed some of the carrier's capacity to sustain operations.

evidence.note: ASV components for replacement Swordfish, a shipboard Martlet folding-wing conversion, and spare wings, engines, and fuselages excluded from air-group totals.

segments.summary: A folding-wing conversion and stocks of spare aircraft components show how carrier workshops supported sustained operations.

segments.title: Carrier aviation in the Madagascar invasion
segments.body: Illustrious and Indomitable supported the Madagascar invasion because Britain feared that French authorities might surrender the island to Japan, following the loss of Indochina. A Japanese foothold there would threaten the shipping route around Africa that supplied Egypt and the North African campaign. Fighting in the Mediterranean had blocked the shorter passage through Suez, forcing supplies onto this longer route. Britain therefore had to sustain the North African campaign around the Cape while trying to reopen the Mediterranean for faster communications with the Far East. Illustrious's aircraft attacked French naval units and protected the invasion force.

evidence.note: The invasion sought to prevent a Japanese foothold threatening the supply route around Africa while the Mediterranean passage remained blocked.

segments.summary: Illustrious supported the Madagascar invasion because control of the island affected Britain's long supply route around Africa.

segments.title: Why Japan's elite naval pilots were hard to replace
segments.body: Japanese naval aviation had limited night-flying capability at this stage because enthusiasts had become concentrated in particular parts of the force and had not spread their training widely. The system produced some exceptionally skilled pilots while keeping that expertise confined. It lacked an effective way to reproduce their skills throughout a larger force. Such concentrated proficiency was difficult to sustain during a long war.

evidence.note: Japan's limited spread of night-flying expertise illustrates the difficulty of reproducing specialist pilot skills throughout the force.

segments.summary: Concentrating specialist night-flying skills in small parts of Japan's naval aviation force made those skills difficult to spread or sustain.

segments.title: Deck parking leaves room to maintain aircraft
segments.body: Illustrious carried 47 aircraft during the Madagascar operations, but sustaining that group required room to work on them. Five Martlets and one Swordfish remained in the deck park to free space below. Packing every aircraft into the hangar could leave no room to unfold wings or carry out necessary maintenance. The workable air group therefore depended on the maintenance that crews needed to perform as well as the number of aircraft that physically fitted.

evidence.note: Six aircraft stayed in the deck park to preserve working space for wing unfolding and hangar maintenance.

segments.summary: Keeping five Martlets and one Swordfish on deck freed the hangar space needed to unfold wings and maintain the air group.

segments.title: Swordfish and Martlets over Diego Suarez
segments.body: Illustrious launched eighteen of her twenty-one Swordfish before dawn alongside eight Martlets, a strong serviceability showing for the biplanes. The single-seat fighters were told to follow the navigator-equipped Swordfish home if they had trouble finding the moving carrier. Swordfish flights carried torpedoes, depth charges, bombs, and leaflets, attacking shipping, two submarines, artillery, and other defences around Diego Suarez. Another Swordfish spotted for naval bombardment, helping the surface ships achieve accurate fire. Radar guidance and the Martlet's better climb rate let controllers exploit interception methods developed with the slower-climbing Fulmar. Martlets intercepted French reconnaissance aircraft and fighters, while Swordfish dropped dummy parachutists as a diversion. The 209 sorties were accompanied by three operational aircraft losses and six deck-landing crashes.

evidence.note: The Madagascar operations combined different Swordfish weapon loads, submarine attacks, gunfire spotting, radar-directed Martlet interceptions, and diversions, with 209 sorties and recorded combat and landing losses.

segments.summary: During the Madagascar operations, Swordfish attacked shipping, submarines, and shore defences while Martlets intercepted French reconnaissance and fighter aircraft.

segments.title: Refit for faster aircraft and the Salerno landings
segments.body: Illustrious conducted deck-landing trials for the Blackburn Firebrand, Fairey Firefly, and Barracuda in February 1943 before entering refit at Birkenhead. New radar, a longer flight deck, and stronger anti-aircraft armament accompanied changes to the arresting gear. Two additional wires aft of the rear lift gave faster aircraft more chances to catch a wire and stop earlier in their landing run. During Operation Avalanche at Salerno, Force H protected the amphibious force against the Italian fleet and covered the escort carriers providing direct support ashore. One Martlet escorted surrendering Italian aircraft to Sicily. A further refit after the operation added more flight-deck area and light anti-aircraft armament.

evidence.note: Deck-landing trials, new radar and armament, two arresting wires aft of the rear lift, and Force H's protective role at Salerno.

segments.summary: A 1943 refit lengthened the flight deck, improved radar and arresting gear, then prepared Illustrious for air cover at Salerno.

segments.title: Operation Governor and Queen Mary escort duty
segments.body: After her 1943 refit trials, Illustrious sailed with Unicorn, Anson, and USS Alabama in Operation Governor. The force was part of Allied efforts to distract Germany while Sicily was the real invasion objective. Its appearance in northern waters also presented a powerful carrier-and-battleship group if Tirpitz came out, though no engagement followed. The ships later escorted RMS Queen Mary while she carried Winston Churchill toward the Quebec Conference, remaining with her through the zone of German air threat. Illustrious returned to Greenock once Queen Mary had passed beyond the range of German aircraft.

evidence.note: In Operation Governor, Illustrious joined a northern surface group intended to divert attention from Sicily, then helped escort Queen Mary toward Quebec.

segments.summary: Illustrious joined a Norwegian Sea diversion intended to complicate Germany's assessment of the Sicily invasion, then protected Queen Mary carrying Churchill toward Quebec.

segments.title: Operation Cockpit attacks Sabang's shore facilities
segments.body: Illustrious joined USS Saratoga for Operation Cockpit against Japanese facilities after returning to the Indian Ocean in 1944. Her air group contained twenty-one Barracudas and twenty-eight Corsairs, with seventeen Barracudas and thirteen Corsairs taking part in the first attack. American aircraft concentrated on harbour shipping while the British force attacked shore installations. The Barracudas destroyed oil-storage tanks and badly damaged port facilities, while twenty-four aircraft were destroyed on the ground. Aerial opposition was slight and every British aircraft returned safely, although one American fighter ditched on the return flight.

evidence.note: Combined operations with Saratoga divided attacks between shipping and shore installations, with oil tanks, port facilities, and aircraft destroyed.

segments.summary: Illustrious's Barracudas and Corsairs attacked shore installations while Saratoga's aircraft concentrated on shipping during Operation Cockpit.

segments.title: Flexible air groups in the Eastern Fleet
segments.body: Somerville wanted another strike before Saratoga left the Indian Ocean for refit, choosing the naval base and refinery at Surabaya. The approach from south of Java put the target beyond the Barracuda's range, so eighteen Avengers replaced the Barracuda squadrons for Operation Transom. Refuelling at Exmouth Gulf made the distant operation possible. Illustrious launched eighteen Avengers and sixteen escorting Corsairs on 17 May, losing one Avenger in a take-off crash; an American Avenger was also shot down over the target. The attack sank only a small ship and inflicted little damage on the refinery. Aircraft selection set the carrier's strike range, a constraint that also applied to later procurement decisions based on expectations of post-Cold War wars of choice. A simulated strike toward Sabang in June was intended to distract Japan from American operations in the Marianas. For the subsequent Port Blair attack, six Barracudas went ashore to make room for fourteen extra Corsairs, another change in the balance between strike aircraft and fighters.

evidence.note: Avengers and Exmouth Gulf refuelling enabled the Surabaya raid, which achieved limited damage, before diversionary operations and an exchange of six Barracudas for fourteen Corsairs.

segments.summary: Replacing Barracudas with Avengers extended Illustrious's strike range for Surabaya, while later operations required a larger fighter group.

segments.title: Why a carrier force needed a spare landing deck
segments.body: The Port Blair strike in the Andaman Islands put more than fifty aircraft in the air while Illustrious was the only available deck on which they could recover. A single landing accident could therefore have trapped the whole force aloft, converting a routine mishap into a mass loss. The arrival of Indomitable and Victorious supplied additional landing decks for large carrier operations. Victorious brought that extra capacity even though her new air wing was not yet considered combat ready despite having experienced leaders.

evidence.note: The risk of losing more than fifty airborne aircraft if the only landing deck became blocked, and the extra decks provided by Indomitable and Victorious despite the latter's air-wing readiness limits.

segments.summary: Launching more than fifty aircraft from one carrier exposed the Eastern Fleet to losing an entire airborne force if a deck accident blocked recovery.

segments.title: Corsairs direct the bombardment at Sabang
segments.body: Operation Crimson used the carriers chiefly for fighter cover, observation, photography, and fleet protection. Illustrious retained roughly nine Barracudas for anti-submarine patrols while Victorious flew off all of hers to make room for fighters. Illustrious launched twenty-two Corsairs to provide combat air patrol, observe naval gunfire, and photograph the results. Their spotting helped the surface ships deliver an effective bombardment by correcting the aim of the heavy guns. Corsairs also intercepted Japanese reconnaissance aircraft and drove off a later group of fighters.

evidence.note: Illustrious's twenty-two Corsairs provided cover, gunfire spotting, and damage-assessment photography while a reduced Barracuda group flew anti-submarine patrols.

segments.summary: At Sabang, Illustrious's fighters spotted and assessed naval bombardment while a small Barracuda force handled anti-submarine patrols.

segments.title: Why Vian chose Indefatigable as his flagship
segments.body: Illustrious joined the First Aircraft Carrier Squadron under Rear Admiral Sir Philip Vian, who flew his flag from Indefatigable. The larger carrier had room for a flag staff and its supporting command facilities, space that a smaller treaty-constrained ship could not spare as easily. Wartime construction and the relaxation of treaty limits had allowed those expanded facilities. The additional space supported the staff needed to command several carriers together.

evidence.note: Vian commanded from Indefatigable because her larger wartime-built hull, freed from treaty constraints, provided better flag facilities.

segments.summary: Indefatigable's larger wartime-built hull offered the staff space needed to command the British Pacific Fleet's carrier squadron.

segments.title: Striking Sumatran oil infrastructure
segments.body: Illustrious joined Operation Outflank with 36 Corsairs and 21 Avengers, then carried 32 Corsairs and 21 Avengers during the Operation Meridian raids on Sumatran oil installations. Her aircraft helped destroy storage tanks and reduce refinery output while the British Pacific Fleet moved toward Sydney. Across the two Meridian attacks, she lost five Corsairs to enemy fighters or flak, another to a mechanical problem on take-off, and three Avengers to enemy action. The raids also exposed weaknesses in fleet air defence when friendly shells struck Illustrious, killing twelve and wounding twenty-one. She subsequently needed repairs in Sydney.

evidence.note: Sumatran refinery strikes, changing air-group totals, nine aircraft lost in the Meridian operations, and subsequent friendly-shell damage requiring Sydney repairs.

segments.summary: Corsairs and Avengers struck Sumatran oil installations, with nine aircraft lost across the two Meridian attacks.

segments.title: An Avenger's unexpected fighter victory
segments.body: One Avenger pilot claimed to have shot down a Nakajima Ki-44 during the Sumatran operations. The circumstances are uncertain, but one account places the fighter in cloud preparing to dive on aircraft below, unaware of the Avenger coming up behind it. That would have given the bomber an exceptional chance to fire first. A related Swordfish example concerns fighters overshooting a much slower opponent and passing into its gunfire. Slowing down and changing the approach could reverse that advantage, so these encounters depended on positioning and tactics.

evidence.note: Uncertain account of an Avenger's claimed Ki-44 victory and comparison with fighter overshoots against Swordfish.

segments.summary: An Avenger pilot's claimed victory during the Sumatra raids shows how surprise and relative position could give a bomber a fleeting advantage over a fighter.

segments.title: Friendly fire exposed an air-defence discipline gap
segments.body: British Pacific Fleet anti-aircraft fire was less disciplined than the practices developed in the Mediterranean. When seven Japanese bombers penetrated the fighter screen, the barrage destroyed every attacker, but shells from either Indomitable or King George V struck Illustrious. Twelve sailors were killed and twenty-one wounded, forcing repairs in Sydney. Dense defensive fire could protect a formation from aircraft while still inflicting serious losses when ships did not coordinate it closely enough.

evidence.note: British Pacific Fleet air defence was less disciplined than the practices developed in the Mediterranean. It destroyed the attacking aircraft but sent friendly shells into Illustrious, killing twelve and wounding twenty-one.

segments.summary: Undisciplined fleet anti-aircraft fire killed twelve men aboard Illustrious even though the attacking Japanese aircraft were destroyed.

segments.title: Okinawa damage ends Illustrious's front-line war
segments.body: Task Force 57 used Illustrious's aircraft to help neutralize airfields in the Sakishima Islands before the Okinawa invasion. She was already limited to 24 knots because vibration from earlier damage had led to removal of the centre propeller. A bomb detonating close alongside damaged aircraft and worsened vibration, although the carrier initially remained operational. Whether the lasting damage affected the hull structure or principally its plating is disputed, with accumulated plating damage offered as the more likely explanation. Divers at San Pedro Bay found split outer plating, and the ship returned to Sydney for repairs. The available facilities could not complete the work, so she returned to Britain in June 1945 for permanent repairs.

evidence.note: Okinawa operations, worsened vibration after a kamikaze near miss, the disputed extent of structural damage, split outer plating, and the return for permanent repair.

segments.summary: A near-miss by a kamikaze attack off Okinawa worsened accumulated hull damage and forced Illustrious out of front-line operations.

segments.title: Illustrious's short postwar jet-carrier career
segments.body: Illustrious continued serving after her front-line war ended. She carried jets and performed postwar duties despite her accumulated damage. Commissioned in 1940 and decommissioned in 1955, she served for fewer than sixteen years. One surviving ship's bell bears heavy damage from her service.

evidence.note: Postwar jet duties, decommissioning in 1955 after commissioning in 1940, and the damaged surviving ship's bell.

segments.summary: Illustrious remained useful for jet work after 1945 and was decommissioned in 1955, fewer than sixteen years after commissioning.

segments.title: Treaty limits and the path to the supercarrier
segments.body: The Midway class used British information to refine American ideas, while Britain's later carrier projects reflected its own response to similar requirements. Protection, striking power, and sufficient fleet numbers were difficult to combine within treaty limits. Carriers of about 27,000 tons standard displacement would have left Britain with only five hulls, even though seven had struggled to meet peacetime commitments. Illustrious and Ark Royal were attempts to obtain the necessary capabilities from smaller ships. American designs would likely continue to place relatively greater emphasis on air-group size, while British designs would favour survivability because of their strategic circumstances. Japan faced a further constraint: nearby bases could not compensate for limited industrial capacity and facilities for replacing heavy losses.

evidence.note: British information helped refine American Midway ideas, while treaty fleet-number arithmetic and different strategic and industrial circumstances shaped converging carrier designs.

segments.summary: Illustrious and Ark Royal show how Britain, the United States, and Japan approached the same carrier problem from different strategic positions.

segments.title: Continental and blue-water carrier design paths
segments.body: Britain, the United States, and Japan followed a different carrier path from concepts emerging in France, Germany, and Italy. Béarn, Joffre, Graf Zeppelin, and related continental projects formed a recognizable alternative family. The distinction rested on institutional experience: navies that had operated carriers extensively were moving toward large but functionally straightforward fleet carriers. Carrier designs can therefore be compared through the doctrine and operating practice behind them as well as their hull dimensions.

evidence.note: British, American, and Japanese carrier development followed a different path from the continental concepts pursued by France, Germany, and Italy.

segments.summary: Britain, the United States, and Japan moved toward large, functionally straightforward fleet carriers, while France, Germany, and Italy pursued a different design family.

segments.title: Would deck-edge lifts have changed Illustrious?
segments.body: Exploratory sketches placed two deck-edge lifts on the starboard side, although the official designs did not adopt them. Larger aircraft would have been easier to handle, and reclaimed internal spaces could have provided additional aircraft or maintenance room. British experience of losing aircraft in North Sea and North Atlantic conditions offered one possible reason for caution. Openings through the hangar's side armour were another concern, while the altered layout would sacrifice office space between the hangar and the hull. Moving the lifts would change the vulnerable areas exposed to bombing, exchanging openings in the flight deck for openings in the side. Their off-centre weight would require ballast and attention to stability. The preference for protection reflected the need to survive repeated air attack and remain repairable far from Britain.

evidence.note: Exploratory starboard deck-edge-lift sketches, possible maintenance-space gains, and proposed reasons for caution involving heavy seas, side protection, and ballast.

segments.summary: Exploratory deck-edge-lift sketches offered more aircraft space but raised concerns about heavy seas, side armour, and stability.

segments.title: Estimating the air group with deck-edge lifts
segments.body: A rough estimate for two deck-edge lifts increases the air group from 36 aircraft to eighteen Fulmars and twenty-four Swordfish. Moving the lifts outboard would free their former positions and adjacent spaces for aircraft, with doors needed to protect the new openings from the sea. Folded aircraft could also occupy space around the lift approaches. A slightly longer hull might be necessary, and the suggested displacement rises to about 24,000 tons standard. These figures are an exploratory estimate, with the final arrangement and usable parking space left uncertain.

evidence.note: Tentative air-group and displacement estimates for the deck-edge-lift alternative, including sea-protection doors and uncertainty over usable space.

segments.summary: A rough counterfactual increases the Fulmar and Swordfish complement from 36 to 42 aircraft by reclaiming internal lift space.
